ex.en: Hello, I'm Michal. And you?

note: Literally "peace". Used both to say hello and to say goodbye, at any time of day.

ex.en: Good morning! Want some coffee?

note: The classic reply is בוקר אור (bóker or, lit. "morning of light"), but answering בוקר טוב is fine too.

ex.en: Good evening, could we have a table for two?

note: A greeting from late afternoon on. It is also said when you leave in the evening (= have a nice evening). Late at night or before bed, say לילה טוב.

ex.en: Good night, kids! Off to bed.

note: Gender surprise: לילה is masculine even though it ends in ה, so it is לילה טוב, not טובה. Plural: לילות.

ex.he: — שלום רונית, מה שלומך? — מצוין, תודה!
ex.en: — Hi Ronit, how are you? — Great, thanks!

note: Lit. "what is your peace?". Written the same for both genders, but said shlomkhá to a man and shlomékh to a woman. To a group: מה שלומכם? (ma shlomkhém). More casual: מה נשמע?

ex.he: — היי, מה נשמע? — הכול טוב, ואצלך?
ex.en: — Hey, how's it going? — All good, and with you?

note: Lit. "what is heard?". The everyday greeting with friends and colleagues; the same form for everyone. Typical answers: בסדר, הכול טוב, סבבה.

ex.en: — Tomorrow at nine? — OK, no problem.

note: Lit. "in order". Answers both "how are you?" (fine) and a suggestion (OK). לא בסדר = not OK, and also "not fair, out of line".

ex.en: Thanks for the help!

note: תודה רבה = thank you very much. To thank for something: תודה על + the thing.

ex.en: Could I have some water, please?

note: Three jobs: "please" when you ask, "here you are" when you hand something over, and "you're welcome" in answer to תודה.

ex.en: — Thank you very much! — You're welcome.

note: Lit. "there's nothing to thank for". A little more polite than בבקשה; in casual speech people also say בכיף or אין בעיה.

ex.en: Goodbye, talk to you tomorrow!

note: Lit. "to see each other" (an infinitive used as a greeting). Casual: ביי or יאללה ביי. נתראה = see you (soon).

ex.he: — אני עמית. — נעים מאוד, אני נדיה.
ex.en: — I'm Amit. — Nice to meet you, I'm Nadia.

note: Said when you are introduced to someone. Reply with נעים מאוד or גם לי (me too). On its own, נעים means "pleasant".

ex.en: Welcome to Israel, Max!

note: Lit. "blessed is the one who comes". It agrees with the person: ברוכה הבאה (to a woman), ברוכים הבאים (to a group), ברוכות הבאות (to women).

ex.he: שלום, קוראים לי אלכס. איך קוראים לך?
ex.en: Hi, my name is Alex. What's your name?

note: Lit. "(they) call me". To ask: איך קוראים לך? (lit. "how do they call you?"). More formal: שמי... = my name is...

ex.en: What's your name?

note: Masculine, but the plural ends in -ot: שמות (shemót). Same spelling as שם (sham) = there. שם פרטי = first name, שם משפחה = surname.

ex.he: — את סטודנטית? — כן, אני לומדת באוניברסיטה.
ex.en: — Are you a student? — Yes, I study at the university.

note: Don't confuse it with כאן (kan) = here.

ex.en: No, I don't live here.

note: Both "no" and "not". It goes right before the word it negates: אני לא יודע = I don't know. לא נכון = not true.

ex.en: Maybe tomorrow? Today I'm busy.

note: אולי כן, אולי לא = maybe yes, maybe no.

ex.en: Who's that? Your brother?

note: With prepositions: של מי? = whose?, עם מי? = with whom? מי זה? / מי זאת? = who is that? (m./f.)

ex.en: What's this? A cake?

note: מה? on its own = what? / sorry? (when you didn't hear). מה זה? = what is this?

ex.en: Where do you live?

note: For direction use לאן? (where to?); for origin, מאיפה? (where from?).

ex.en: — Where are you from? — I'm from Haifa.

note: מ + איפה. The answer takes מ too: מחיפה, מרוסיה, מאתיופיה, מצרפת.

ex.en: Where are you going on Saturday?

note: Used with verbs of movement (ללכת, לנסוע). In casual speech you may hear לאיפה, but לאן is the standard form.

ex.en: When is the lesson? At ten?

note: For questions, including indirect ones: אני לא יודע מתי = I don't know when. For "when" in a statement, use כש־ (kshe-): כשאני בבית... = when I'm at home...

ex.en: Why are you sad?

note: Answer with כי (because): כי אני עייף. Formal and written: מדוע.

ex.en: How do you say this in Hebrew?

note: איך קוראים לך? = what's your name? איך היה? = how was it?

ex.en: How many children do you have?

note: Also "a few" before a noun: כמה דקות = a few minutes. כמה זה עולה? = how much does it cost?

ex.en: What day is it today?

note: Standard forms: איזה (m.), איזו (éizo, f.), אילו (éilu, pl.); in casual speech איזה often covers all three. As an exclamation: איזה כיף! = how nice!

ex.he: אני סטודנט, ואני גר בבאר שבע.
ex.en: I'm a student, and I live in Be'er Sheva.

note: There is no word for "am/is/are" in the present: אני סטודנט = I (am a) student.

ex.en: Are you a teacher? Me too!

note: To one man. To one woman: את. Hebrew has no polite "you", so אתה is fine even with your boss.

ex.en: Do you want tea or coffee?

note: To one woman. Same spelling as the object marker את (et), which has no English equivalent: אני רואה את הים. Context tells them apart.

ex.en: This is Yosef. He's my brother.

note: Also "it" for masculine things: — איפה הטלפון? — הוא על השולחן.

ex.en: This is Rachel. She's a doctor.

note: Also "it" for feminine things: — איפה העוגה? — היא במקרר.

ex.he: אנחנו מרוסיה, ועכשיו אנחנו גרים בחולון.
ex.en: We're from Russia, and now we live in Holon.

note: Formal and written: אנו (ánu).

ex.en: Are you hungry? There's pizza.

note: To a group of men or a mixed group. To women only: אתן.

ex.en: Girls, are you ready?

note: Only for a group of women. In everyday speech many people use אתם for women too, but the standard form is אתן.

ex.he: ההורים שלי בבית. הם לא עובדים היום.
ex.en: My parents are at home. They aren't working today.

note: For men or a mixed group. For women only: הן.

ex.he: ליאת ורים חברות. הן לומדות ביחד.
ex.en: Liat and Rim are friends. They study together.

note: Only for an all-female group. In casual speech הם often replaces הן.

ex.en: This is my house.

note: For masculine nouns, and for "it/that" in general: זה טוב = that's good. After a noun it means "this": הבית הזה = this house.

ex.en: This is my mother, Dina.

note: For feminine nouns. זו means the same and is a little more formal. After a noun: הדירה הזאת = this apartment.

ex.en: These are our children.

note: The same for both genders. אלו (élu) means the same. After a noun: הספרים האלה = these books.

ex.en: I'm from Tel Aviv. You too?

note: It goes before the word it refers to: גם אני = me too. גם... וגם... = both... and...

ex.en: I only have ten shekels.

note: It comes before the word it limits. רק רגע = just a moment.

ex.en: I can't talk now.

note: Related words: כרגע = at the moment, for now; מיד = right away.

ex.en: My office is here, on the second floor.

note: כאן (kan) means the same and is a bit more formal. מפה / מכאן = from here.

ex.en: The bank is there, next to the supermarket.

note: Same spelling as שם (shem) = name. משם = from there.

ex.en: The apartment is small but very nice.

note: With adjectives it can go before or after: מאוד יפה = יפה מאוד. With verbs it goes after: אני אוהב את זה מאוד. The older spelling מאד is also seen.

ex.en: Everything's fine, thanks.

note: Also spelled הכל. Without ה, כל + noun = every / all: כל יום = every day, כל הילדים = all the children.

ex.en: Can I have another glass of water?

note: עוד + noun = more / another; עוד לא = not yet; מה עוד? = what else?

ex.en: I have a brother and two sisters.

note: Hebrew has no verb "to have": יש לי = I have (lit. "there is to me"), יש לך = you have. The negative is אין.

ex.en: I don't have time today.

note: The negative of יש: אין לי = I don't have. אין בעיה = no problem.

ex.en: This is Danny's bag.

note: The owner comes after the thing: הספר של נועה = Noa's book. With endings: שלי (mine), שלך (yours), שלו (his), שלה (hers), שלנו (ours).

ex.en: I have a big family.

note: "My family": המשפחה שלי, or more formally משפחתי (mishpakhtí).

ex.en: My dad works at a bank.

note: Masculine even though it ends in an -a sound. Often used like a name, without ה: אבא בבית = Dad is home. The formal word is אב; plural אבות.

ex.en: My mother is from Ethiopia.

note: Like אבא, often used as a name without ה. The formal word is אם (em); plural אמהות (imahót), with an extra ה.

ex.en: My parents live in Jerusalem.

note: Usually plural. The singular הורה (horé) = a parent exists but is less common in everyday speech: כל הורה יודע את זה = every parent knows that.

ex.he: יש לי אח קטן. הוא בן שש.
ex.en: I have a little brother. He's six.

note: אחים = brothers, or siblings of both genders. Also means a male nurse. Colloquially, אחי (akhí) = bro.

ex.en: My sister studies at the university.

note: Irregular plural: אחיות (akhayót). Also means a nurse: האחות במרפאה = the nurse at the clinic.

ex.en: They have a son and a daughter.

note: Also used for age: הוא בן עשר = he is ten (lit. "a son of ten"). בנים = sons, and also boys in general.

ex.en: Our daughter is in first grade.

note: Irregular plural: בנות (banót) = daughters, girls. For age: היא בת שבע = she is seven.

ex.en: The boy is playing in the park.

note: ילדים = children of both genders. Same root as יום הולדת (birthday).

ex.he: יש לנו ילדה מתוקה בת שלוש.
ex.en: We have a sweet three-year-old girl.

note: The plural ילדות (yeladót) is spelled like ילדות (yaldút) = childhood.

ex.en: Quiet, the baby's sleeping!

note: A masculine noun with a feminine-looking plural: תינוקות (tinokót). A baby girl: תינוקת.

ex.en: My grandpa is ninety.

note: Like אבא: masculine despite the -a ending, and used as a name without ה. Grandparents: סבא וסבתא, or סבים וסבתות.

ex.en: On Fridays we eat at Grandma's.

note: אצל סבתא = at Grandma's (place). Plural: סבתות (savtót).

ex.en: They have five grandchildren.

note: Granddaughter: נכדה (nekhdá). נכדים = grandchildren of both genders.

ex.en: My husband works in high-tech.

note: "My husband" is usually בעלי (ba'alí); in casual speech also הבעל שלי. The word also means "owner" (בעל הבית = landlord, owner of the house), so some people prefer בן זוג (partner).

ex.en: That woman is my manager.

note: Irregular plural: נשים (nashím). "My wife": אשתי (ishtí) or האישה שלי.

ex.en: That man is our neighbor.

note: Irregular plural: אנשים (anashím) = people. In speech, גבר or בחור are more common for "a man".

ex.he: בצוות שלנו יש שלוש נשים ושני גברים.
ex.en: Our team has three women and two men.

note: The everyday word for an adult man. On restroom doors: גברים / נשים. Same root as גברת (Mrs., lady).

ex.en: This is Omer, a friend of mine from work.

note: Female friend / girlfriend: חברה (khaverá), spelled like חברה (khevrá) = company. החבר שלי usually means "my boyfriend", while חבר שלי = a friend of mine. Also "member": חבר במועדון.

ex.en: Our neighbor is very nice.

note: Feminine: שכנה (shkhená). Same root as שכונה (neighborhood).

ex.en: My aunt lives in Canada.

note: Uncle: דוד (dod), plural דודים. It is spelled the same as דוד (dud) = water heater.

ex.en: I have a cousin in Berlin.

note: Lit. "son of an uncle", but used for any male cousin. A female cousin: בת דודה (or בת דוד). Cousins: בני דודים.

ex.en: Do you have a partner?

note: Female partner: בת זוג. A neutral, very common word for a husband or wife, boyfriend or girlfriend. בני זוג = a couple.

ex.he: — אתה נשוי? — כן, ויש לנו שני ילדים.
ex.en: — Are you married? — Yes, and we have two children.

note: Feminine: נשואה (nesu'á); plural: נשואים. Married to: נשוי ל־ (נשוי לרינה = married to Rina).

ex.en: He's single and lives alone.

note: Feminine: רווקה (ravaká). Also a noun: רווק = a bachelor. On forms, the options are usually רווק, נשוי, גרוש, אלמן (widowed).

ex.he: הוא גרוש ויש לו שני בנים.
ex.en: He's divorced and has two sons.

note: Feminine: גרושה (grushá). Don't confuse it with גרוש (grush), an old small coin: אין לי גרוש = I don't have a penny.

ex.en: He's a very nice guy.

note: Feminine: בחורה (bakhurá) = young woman. Very common in speech: אחלה בחור = a great guy.

ex.he: — בן כמה אתה? — אני בן שלושים.
ex.en: — How old are you? — I'm thirty.

note: Lit. "son of how many are you?". To a woman: בת כמה את? The answer uses the feminine form of the number for everyone (because שנים is feminine): בן שלוש, בת שלוש.

ex.en: We have the same last name.

note: On forms: שם פרטי (first name) and שם משפחה. With "the", the ה goes on the second word: שם המשפחה.

ex.he: בגיל שש ילדים הולכים לכיתה א׳.
ex.en: At age six, children start first grade.

note: בגיל + number = at the age of: בגיל עשרים. Gil is also a common Israeli first name.

ex.en: Happy birthday, Grandma!

note: With "the", the ה goes on the second word: יום ההולדת. Plural: ימי הולדת. Same root as ילד (child).

ex.en: Mr. Levy, the doctor is waiting for you.

note: Addressing a man directly: אדוני (adoní) = sir. In writing the title is usually מר (Mr.): מר לוי. Feminine: גברת.

ex.en: Mrs. Avraham, do you have a question?

note: Used before a surname or on its own to address a woman politely; גברתי (gvirtí) = madam. גבירותיי ורבותיי = ladies and gentlemen.

ex.en: Guys, the food is ready!

note: Plural in meaning and takes a plural verb: החבר׳ה מהעבודה באים = the people from work are coming. Used for mixed groups too.

ex.en: He's a good person.

note: The everyday word for "a person", used for women too (היא בן אדם טוב). Plural: בני אדם = people, human beings. In casual writing: בנאדם.
